summary:
magine being millions of kilometres from everyone you love, and feeling yourself slip. You sleep badly. You react slower. Mission control asks how you are, and you say what every astronaut says: “I’m fine.” It isn’t true, and no one can tell.

On the way to Mars, help is up to twenty minutes away, and no doctor is coming. The body is watched closely. The mind is far easier to miss. In a crew that small, losing one mind can mean losing the mission.

Hearth exists so that never happens unseen.

Designed as an added feature for the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor smart shirt, Hearth adds the mind to the body. It learns who each astronaut is on Earth, before launch. Then, every day in flight, it quietly checks how they feel and how they perform against that person, not against an average. When it sees a lasting change, it tells them what is happening, what to try, and who to turn to. It works with no link to Earth, and the astronaut decides what anyone else sees.

Hearth does not diagnose. It notices, when no one on Earth can.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Hearth adds the mind to astronaut health monitoring. It is designed as an added feature for the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor shirt, which already tracks the body.

Before launch: Hearth learns each astronaut’s own normal on Earth, and a flight surgeon signs it off.

In flight: one locked personal offset accounts for the body adapting to space. Mood, stress and reaction time get no offset, so feeling worse never becomes “normal”.

Every day: the astronaut rates mood, stress and workload and takes a reaction test, modelled on the self-test astronauts completed 2,856 times on the space station.

When something changes: one bad day is ignored. A pattern on four of the last five days is flagged, and Hearth says what changed, what to try and who should act: the astronaut, the crew medical officer or the flight surgeons.

With no link to Earth: every calculation runs on the device. What the astronaut chooses to share syncs to the ground when the link returns.

What benefits does it have?

It catches what self-report misses. The reaction test does not depend on what the astronaut chooses to say.

It is personal. Each astronaut is compared with their own normal, not a crew average.

It works alone. A month without contact loses nothing.

It is private. The astronaut switches each kind of data on or off and sees everyone who looked at it.

It is cheap to adopt. It builds on hardware that has already flown, not a new device.

What is the intended impact?

On a Mars mission, help is up to twenty minutes away each way and a small crew cannot afford to lose one mind. Hearth aims to make psychological decline visible early, onboard, so the crew can act before it becomes a mission risk. In tests on 1,000 simulated astronauts it caught 99.6% of the declines we injected.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Software: a website that works offline and installs like an app, plus a ground service and flight-surgeon console, running as one Docker image with PostgreSQL and optional Caddy for https.

Hardware: any device with a modern browser, a Bluetooth heart-rate strap (Chrome or Edge) and a microphone.

Demo videos: Python with Pillow, PyAV (FFmpeg) and NumPy; Whisper, run locally, to time the captions.

AI tools: Claude (Anthropic) for code, documents and scripts.

To add: the app’s coding languages and frameworks. I don’t have the app’s source, so I can’t name them.

How is your project creative?

A normal from Earth, adjusted once. Most monitoring learns a baseline in flight. Hearth sets it on Earth and applies one locked offset, which cut false alarms from nearly every healthy simulated astronaut to under a third.

The mind is never excused. Body readings get an offset for space; mood, stress and reaction time deliberately do not.

The device decides; the ground observes. This reverses today’s model, where data goes to Earth to be interpreted.

The astronaut sees who looked. Every read by ground staff is logged and shown to them.

What factors did your team consider?

Communication delay and blackouts: nothing may depend on Earth.

Crew time: the check-in takes about five minutes.

False alarms against missed problems: we measured the trade-off and chose a threshold; the final choice needs a clinician.

The body’s adaptation to space: without the offset, almost every healthy astronaut looked unwell.

Privacy and trust: this is health data about named people.

Accessibility: every status has its own shape as well as a colour.

Honesty about limits: the mission data is simulated, the thresholds are placeholders, there is no link to Bio-Monitor yet, and Hearth supports decisions without diagnosing.
